text: Apache Spark uses lazy evaluation: transformations like map(), filter(), and select() build a logical plan but do not execute until an action (collect(), count(), write()) is called. The Catalyst optimizer analyzes the full plan before execution, enabling it to reorder filters, eliminate redundant steps, and combine shuffle operations. This means calling df.filter(...).map(...) does not move any data — it only records the intent. The physical plan is only generated and executed when an action triggers it.

Spark partitioning determines parallelism. A DataFrame's default partition count is set by spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (default 200) for shuffles. For reads, the number of input partitions depends on the source: HDFS files produce one partition per 128MB block by default, Kafka sources produce one partition per Kafka partition. You can repartition() to increase or coalesce() to decrease partitions without a full shuffle. Skewed partitions — where one partition has far more data than others — cause stragglers and slow the entire job.

An Apache Airflow DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) defines a workflow as a Python file. Tasks within the DAG are connected with >> (bitshift operator) to set dependencies: task_a >> task_b means task_b runs after task_a succeeds. The scheduler reads DAG files on a configurable interval and triggers runs based on the schedule_interval. DAG runs are identified by their logical date (formerly execution_date), which represents the start of the schedule interval, not the actual time the run was triggered.

Airflow XComs (cross-communications) allow tasks to share small amounts of data. A task pushes a value with xcom_push(key, value) or by returning a value from execute(). Downstream tasks pull it with xcom_get(task_id, key). XComs are stored in the Airflow metadata database and are suitable only for small values (strings, numbers, small dicts) — not DataFrames or large files. For large data transfer between tasks, store the data in an external system (S3, GCS, a database) and pass only the path or reference as an XCom.

Delta Lake adds ACID transactions to data lakes. Every write (insert, update, delete, merge) is recorded in the transaction log (_delta_log directory) as a JSON commit file. Readers see a consistent snapshot by reading the transaction log to determine which Parquet files are part of the current table version. This enables time travel: you can query a table as it existed at a past version or timestamp. ACID guarantees mean concurrent writes do not corrupt the table — conflicting writes are detected and one is retried or rejected.

dbt (data build tool) organizes SQL transformations into three conventional layers. The staging layer selects from raw source tables and applies basic cleaning (casting, renaming, filtering nulls) without joining. The intermediate layer joins and enriches staged data. The mart layer produces analytics-ready tables (facts and dimensions) designed for BI tools. Each layer is a separate subdirectory in models/. This separation makes transformations independently testable and prevents downstream consumers from depending on unstable raw data shapes.

dbt data quality tests run assertions against model output. Generic tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) are configured in YAML schema files. Singular tests are custom SQL queries that return rows when a condition fails — if any rows are returned, the test fails. Tests run with dbt test and can be configured to warn or error. dbt also supports source freshness checks: source freshness defines a maximum age for source tables, and dbt source freshness alerts when a table has not been updated within the threshold.

A Kafka consumer group allows multiple consumers to share the work of reading from a topic. Each partition in the topic is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group at a time. If a group has more consumers than partitions, some consumers sit idle. Adding consumers to a group (up to the partition count) increases throughput linearly. Kafka tracks each consumer group's read position (offset) per partition in an internal topic called __consumer_offsets. Consumer groups enable independent processing: two different groups can each read all messages from the same topic independently.

Within a single Kafka partition, messages are strictly ordered by offset. Across partitions, there is no ordering guarantee. When a producer sends messages without a key, Kafka distributes them across partitions in round-robin order. When a key is specified, Kafka hashes the key and always routes messages with the same key to the same partition, preserving order for that key. This is why user_id is a common partition key for event streams: all events for the same user land in the same partition and are processed in order.

BigQuery table partitioning divides a table into segments by a column value, typically a date or timestamp. Queries that filter on the partition column scan only the matching partitions, reducing both cost and latency. Clustering further sorts data within each partition by one or more columns; clustered queries scan only the relevant byte ranges within a partition. Partitioning prunes at the partition level (whole partitions skipped); clustering prunes at the block level within partitions. Both can be applied together: partition by date, cluster by user_id or region.

Apache Flink distinguishes event-time from processing-time. Processing-time assigns events to windows based on the system clock when the event is processed by Flink. Event-time assigns events to windows based on a timestamp embedded in the event itself. For analytics that must reflect when something actually happened — user purchases, sensor readings, clickstream events — event-time is correct. Processing-time is simpler to implement but produces wrong aggregates whenever events arrive late or out of order, which is common in any system with retry queues, network lag, or upstream batch flushes.

Flink watermarks signal event-time progress to the streaming engine. A watermark at time T means: all events with timestamp <= T have been observed. When a window's end time is <= the current watermark, the window closes and results are emitted. BoundedOutOfOrderness watermarks tolerate late events by subtracting a configured lag from the maximum observed event timestamp. For example, a 30-second lag means Flink waits an extra 30 seconds before closing each window, absorbing events that arrive up to 30 seconds late. Events arriving after the window closes can be routed to a side output rather than silently dropped.

Snowflake stores data in micro-partitions: immutable, compressed columnar files of 50–500MB of uncompressed data. Snowflake automatically tracks the min and max value of each column in each micro-partition in metadata. At query time, Snowflake uses this metadata to skip micro-partitions that cannot contain rows matching the filter — a process called micro-partition pruning. This is why filters on columns with high cardinality and monotonic values (like timestamps or incrementing IDs) are especially efficient: they prune most micro-partitions immediately.

A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system grounds LLM responses in retrieved documents. At query time: (1) the user question is embedded or matched against a document corpus; (2) the top-k most relevant document chunks are retrieved; (3) the chunks are included in the LLM prompt as context; (4) the LLM generates an answer constrained to that context. RAG reduces hallucination on factual questions because the model reasons over retrieved evidence rather than relying on parametric (baked-in) knowledge. The quality of a RAG system depends on both retrieval quality and faithfulness of the generation step.

Prompt caching (supported by Anthropic and some other providers) stores a processed version of a prompt prefix on the provider's servers. On subsequent API calls that share the same prefix, the cached prefix is reused rather than reprocessed, reducing both latency and cost. Anthropic's implementation uses cache_control with type ephemeral on content blocks to mark them as cacheable. Cached input tokens are billed at approximately 10% of normal input token cost. The cache is keyed on exact content — any change to the cached block invalidates it. Caching is most effective when a large system prompt is stable across many requests.

Spark's DataFrame API supports two execution modes: pandas API on Spark (pyspark.pandas) executes eagerly for compatibility with pandas semantics, while the native DataFrame API remains lazy. Mixing the two without care leads to unexpected eager materialization, since an eager pandas-on-Spark call can force a plan to execute far earlier than a developer used to lazy Spark DataFrames would expect.

Spark Structured Streaming also supports watermarking to bound state size: withWatermark(eventTimeCol, delayThreshold) tells Spark how long to wait for late data before dropping state for a given window, similar in spirit to Flink's watermarks but implemented independently in Spark's own streaming engine rather than Flink's.

Prefect flows pass data between tasks directly as Python return values, since Prefect tracks task dependencies through a DAG built from function calls rather than a separate metadata-database push/pull step like Airflow's XComs. A Prefect task's return value is simply available to whatever downstream task references it in the flow function.

Redshift sort keys determine the physical order rows are stored on disk, similar in effect to BigQuery clustering but implemented via a COPY/VACUUM-driven sort rather than automatic background reclustering. Redshift distribution keys additionally control which node a row lives on, a concept BigQuery's serverless architecture does not expose directly to users.

Great Expectations defines data quality suites as JSON expectation configs run against a dataframe or SQL table, independent of dbt's own model layering. Teams often run Great Expectations checkpoints in the same Airflow DAG that triggers dbt run, validating a mart table only after the staging, intermediate, and mart pipeline stages have all completed successfully.

HTTP caching headers like Cache-Control and ETag let a browser or CDN reuse a previous response without recontacting the origin server. This is a transport-layer optimization distinct from an LLM provider's prompt caching, which caches the model's internal key-value attention state for a prompt prefix rather than caching a full HTTP response body.

Kinesis shards are Kafka's rough equivalent of partitions: each shard supports a fixed read/write throughput. A Kinesis consumer application using the Enhanced Fan-Out API gets a dedicated throughput pipe per shard, rather than sharing a shard's aggregate throughput across a polling consumer group the way a Kafka consumer group does.

Apache Iceberg tracks table state as a sequence of immutable snapshot metadata files rather than Delta Lake's JSON commit log. Iceberg's time travel works by pointing a read at a specific snapshot-id, achieving a similar time-travel capability to Delta Lake's through a different manifest-file-based metadata layout instead of a transaction log directory.

Fine-tuning an LLM on a proprietary dataset bakes new facts directly into the model's parametric weights, which can reduce hallucination on that specific domain but requires retraining whenever the underlying facts change — unlike RAG, which reduces hallucination by grounding answers in retrieved context that can be updated without touching the model's weights at all.

Salting a skewed join key by appending a random suffix to the key before the shuffle spreads what would have been one hot partition across several smaller ones, at the cost of an extra post-join aggregation step needed to merge the salted groups back together into the original key's result.

BigQuery's columnar storage similarly benefits from filtering on low-cardinality clustered columns, but BigQuery does not expose per-block min/max metadata to users the way Snowflake's micro-partition pruning does. Instead, BigQuery's query planner performs comparable pruning internally without surfacing a user-facing pruning statistic.
